overview: The atlas label “Samoyèdes” is a later outsider umbrella, not the name of a state that ruled this enormous Lower Ob, Yamal, Yenisei, and western Taymyr polygon. Modern Samoyedic describes a branch of Uralic languages that includes distinct Nenets, Enets, Nganasan, Selkup, and extinct varieties. Speech, ancestry, pottery, and political belonging cannot be made identical from one map color. For 700 to 800, the closest dated evidence comes from local archaeological traditions, especially eighth- and ninth-century Kuchimino and related Orontur-type sites in western Siberia, plus more scattered Arctic finds. Semi-subterranean houses, hearths, decorated pottery, iron tools, bone implements, bronze ornaments, graves, hunting, fishing, limited regional reindeer use, and exchange show skilled communities adapting differently to taiga, forest-tundra, rivers, and coast. Evidence is uneven: a Lower Ob house cannot stand for Taymyr, and later Nenets herding cannot be carried backward automatically. No securely localized Samoyedic-language text survives from this century. At 800, the exact id disappears and the atlas restores a broader forest label over every target probe. That seam is editorial, not an extinction, conquest, or clean division into the much later named peoples.

periods.title: 700 to 712: an evidence slice, not a new kingdom
periods.summary: The atlas begins its label at 700, but archaeological chronologies span broad centuries. Orontur-type sites run from about the sixth through ninth centuries, while the Kuchimino grouping is chiefly eighth to ninth century. The opening year therefore organizes the map; it does not record a coronation or migration day.

periods.title: 712 to 725: Taymyr evidence stays sparse and local
periods.summary: Taymyr archaeology preserves long sequences, but first-millennium evidence is thin, unevenly excavated, and difficult to connect with named languages. Pottery and site layers can reveal contact or movement without identifying a household as Nenets, Enets, or Nganasan centuries before those exact atlas records begin.

periods.title: 725 to 737: fortified plans show organized local work
periods.summary: In the Surgut Ob region, Kuchimino forts used rectangular plans, deep ditches, ramparts, and small rows of buildings facing an interior passage. Such construction required coordination and remembered design. It supports local leadership and cooperation, but not one government over the full Arctic polygon.

periods.title: 737 to 750: objects mark chronology better than ethnicity
periods.summary: Archaeologists define the Kuchimino phase largely through vessel form, decoration, and associated finds. Bronze fittings and animal-shaped ornaments help order graves and settlements through time. They are excellent chronological clues, yet no buckle can announce its owner’s language or turn a material grouping into one nation.

periods.title: 750 to 762: river terraces shape what survives
periods.summary: Northern site surveys find many medieval traces on lower river terraces and far fewer in some uplands. That pattern mixes past choices with modern discovery conditions. Rivers mattered, but archaeologists also see what erosion, construction, permafrost, and survey routes allow them to see, so blank areas are not empty histories.

periods.title: 762 to 775: short occupations refine the sequence
periods.summary: Rescue excavations have identified short-lived, single-layer settlements that help separate objects mixed together at longer-used sites. These small places can revise regional chronologies precisely because they contain fewer overlapping occupations. They still document particular visits or households, not a uniform century across Yamal and the Yenisei.

periods.title: 775 to 787: local traditions meet wider exchange
periods.summary: Late eighth-century communities used iron knives and points, bone tools, cast ornaments, and decorated pots while receiving or imitating objects linked westward and southward. Exchange moved materials, designs, and stories across long distances. Shared styles demonstrate contact, not identical speech, ancestry, or political submission.

periods.title: 787 to 800: the map endpoint is not a human ending
periods.summary: Nothing in the archaeological sequence selects 800 as a collapse. Sites and material traditions continue into the ninth century, and later categories change again. The exact atlas id simply vanishes at its indexed endpoint, with every fixed target probe returning to a broad forest label in the next snapshot.

sections.title: What this map feature actually contains

items.text: The index contains one exact samoyedes record, dated approximately 700 to 800, with no summary or card. Coverage calls it a state and queues it to Europe, but the decoded shape lies east of the Urals. A researched override should classify it as an Asian cultural umbrella.

The target appears once, only in world-700. Its single polygon has one ring and 320 positions, spanning roughly 65.23 to 113.72 degrees east and 61.35 to 77.59 degrees north. Those coordinates are a modern editorial envelope, not a surveyed medieval frontier.

Thirteen representative probes from Salekhard and Yamal through Nadym, the Taz, lower Yenisei, Norilsk, western Taymyr, and Khatanga fall inside. Naryan-Mar, Surgut, Khanty-Mansiysk, Tura, Tiksi, and Yakutsk remain outside. Membership tests locate the polygon; they cannot identify a site’s language.

At 700 the target directly shares decoded arcs with the atlas’s Finno-Ugric taiga hunter-gatherer and Paleo-Siberian hunter-gatherer features. These are neighboring editorial categories, not evidence that three uniform peoples met along a mutually recognized border marked by posts, guards, or customs desks.

At 800 every target probe is repainted as Finno-Ugric taiga hunter-gatherers, and the exact id remains absent afterward. The software has changed categories. It has not demonstrated that communities vanished, changed language together, accepted a new ruler, or received a synchronized identity memo.

sections.title: Names, languages, and people are not interchangeable

items.text: “Samoyedes” reflects a later outsider classification. The Indigenous-peoples atlas shows that Russian and scholarly naming later sorted distinct Nenets, Enets, Nganasan, and Selkup communities under changing terms. This card keeps the exact id for software association while using respectful language in its teaching text.

Samoyedic is useful as a language-family term, but the family contains several languages and language complexes. Tundra and Forest Nenets differ substantially; Enets also divides; Selkup contains multiple regional groups. A family relationship does not mean everyone in 700 spoke one standardized tongue.

Northern Samoyedic history includes sustained contact and dialect continua, not only clean splits on a family tree. Contact can spread sounds, words, and grammatical patterns across related communities. That makes the atlas’s hard polygon especially poor evidence for one language boundary or one moment of separation.

Dating language divergence requires explicit calibrations, often from loans or written evidence, and published Uralic estimates remain sensitive to those choices. Since no exact-period Samoyedic text anchors this polygon, assigning a precise 700 dialect map would give the calendar more confidence than the evidence deserves.

Forest Enets traditions preserve family and clan distinctions, and the institutional language atlas notes that even a single later ethnic label can conceal different speech histories. That later evidence does not identify seventh-century residents, but it warns us against treating “Samoyedes” as one household writ continent-sized.

sections.title: Archaeology supplies local clues, not passports

items.text: Orontur-type archaeology covers taiga and tundra sites from the Lower and Middle Ob toward Yamal, with isolated finds farther east and west. Scholars divide it into earlier Zelenaya Gorka and later Kuchimino groupings. These are analytical types built from material patterns, not recorded tribal federations.

The Lower Ob sequence is reconstructed from changing vessel shapes, ornament, settlements, and graves. Similarity can show learned craft traditions and connections; difference can mark time or locality. Neither automatically maps onto a spoken language, and the same community can adopt a neighbor’s useful or attractive design.

Taymyr’s first-millennium record is much thinner than the Lower Ob record. The Smithsonian synthesis compares ceramic traditions and stratified sites while stressing chronological gaps. A sparse peninsula should not be filled with details borrowed from a better-excavated southern house simply because both lie inside one polygon.

Short-term settlements with a single main occupation can sharpen chronology because later rebuilding has not mixed as many deposits. Northern rescue archaeology uses such sites to revise older sequences. Even a wonderfully tidy layer remains one place and season; it does not become a census of the Arctic.

Modern excavation also follows roads, pipelines, eroding banks, and places where surveys are funded. The map’s broad blank or colored zones therefore should not be read as equal archaeological coverage. Absence of a reported house may mean no house, no preservation, or simply no trench.

Excavated Orontur-type dwellings include rectangular semi-subterranean post-built houses of roughly 25 to 70 square meters. Central hearths, earthen sleeping platforms, and corridor entrances appear in published descriptions. They show substantial household labor, but floor area alone cannot reveal an exact family tree.

Some polar settlements used round semi-subterranean houses up to about seven meters across with central hearths. The contrast with rectangular Lower Ob buildings matters: architecture varied with region, season, available materials, and tradition. The atlas therefore cannot issue everyone the same imaginary Arctic starter home.

Kuchimino forts could arrange two to ten structures in facing rows around an interior way, enclosed by ditch and rampart. Repeated proportions suggest learned building rules and coordinated work. Defense and order are visible; the name, powers, and inheritance rules of any leader are not.

Hearths provided heat, light, cooking, and a focus for work inside cold-climate houses. Smoke management, fuel gathering, and fire tending demanded knowledge and attention. Published plans identify hearths, but they do not assign those tasks by gender or age, so the card leaves the chore chart open.

A settlement can be seasonal and still contain carefully built structures, storage, and repeated activity. Northern archaeology records both short occupations and longer-lived fortified places. Mobility is therefore not the opposite of architecture; people can move through a known landscape and return to houses that anchor part of the year.

Animal bone, fishing equipment, hunting weapons, and settlement location support mixed hunting and fishing in much of the western Siberian evidence. The exact balance depended on river, forest, tundra, coast, and season. One menu cannot cover Salekhard, the Taz, Norilsk, and Khatanga without turning geography into soup.

Orontur-type finds include iron and bone arrowheads, knives, and hide-working tools, while the synthesis identifies hunting, fishing, and fur procurement. Northern sites also suggest some reindeer keeping and marine-mammal hunting. Those activities were regional additions, not proof of universal large-herd pastoralism in 700.

Rivers linked camps, fishing places, forests, and exchange routes. Most fixed probes inside the polygon cluster around the Ob, Taz, Yenisei, and their Arctic approaches. Boats are plausible in this river world, but the reviewed exact-period publications do not justify one boat design or ownership rule everywhere.

Taymyr evidence reflects adaptation to extreme seasonality and access to wild resources, yet its occupation history includes movement and long gaps. Modern Nganasan or Nenets routes cannot simply be copied onto the eighth century. Similar environmental problems can produce useful parallels without proving direct continuity of every practice.

Later Nenets, Enets, Nganasan, and Selkup communities developed sharply different combinations of reindeer keeping, fishing, hunting, and settlement. Their diversity is a reminder, not a template for 700. The exact card therefore describes archaeologically supported activities locally and refuses to hand every household a giant herd.

Round-bottomed pots and bowls carried grooves, ridges, comb impressions, and figured stamps. Decoration organized surfaces while vessel form served cooking and storage. Archaeologists use those choices to build chronologies and connections. A patterned pot is both practical technology and visual skill, even when its maker’s name is gone.

Iron knives, spearheads, arrowheads, and tongs show smithing and maintenance, while clay crucibles point to nonferrous metalwork. Production required fuel, heat control, material knowledge, and repeated practice. Finding finished objects does not mean every settlement smelted ore, so workshop claims stay attached to actual evidence.

Bronze ornaments included bird and animal forms, buckles, bracelets, pendants, and decorated knife fittings. Some objects accompanied burials and some circulated in daily life. Their imagery may have carried social or ritual meaning, but assigning one mythology to the whole polygon would outrun the surviving context.

Orontur-type sites contain imported or imitated forms linked with the Kama region, Central Asia, and Iranian metal traditions. Such objects reveal far-reaching chains of exchange rather than a traveler completing the entire route. Materials and designs can pass through many hands, languages, and communities.

Bone awls, handles, spoons, arrowheads, and hide-smoothing implements preserve skilled work beyond metal. Organic tools often survive unevenly, especially outside frozen deposits, so stone and bronze can look unfairly glamorous. Much daily technology was probably made from materials that decay before archaeologists arrive.

Houses with hearths, platforms, tools, and stored goods were social spaces, but archaeology rarely labels the relationships among occupants. A building might hold a nuclear family, extended kin, guests, workers, or changing seasonal groups. The safest language is household, followed by an honest question mark about genealogy.

Paired and collective graves occur in the later Orontur sequence, and some burials contain tools, ornaments, or weapons. These choices show relationships among mourners, bodies, objects, and remembered places. They cannot by themselves identify marriage rules, clans, or a simple ranking system shared across every cemetery.

Children certainly lived in these communities, but the exact-period publications consulted do not provide a secure child-specific assemblage for the whole target. A Gydan infant burial with hair, bone, jewelry, and an imported bowl dates about 900 to 1100, so it belongs to later comparison, not this card’s proof.

No school building, textbook, or written lesson survives from 700 to 800 here. Children likely learned speech, routes, fishing, fire care, craft, weather, and social obligations by watching and participating, but the exact teaching arrangements remain unrecorded. The card calls this plausible learning, not a reconstructed curriculum.

Modern Indigenous language records show multilingual families and highly local speech histories, but those records are centuries later. They demonstrate why learning cannot be reduced to one inherited language across the polygon. In 700, children may have heard several varieties, yet the number and combinations remain unknown.

Early medieval skeletal studies in western Siberia combine small cemetery samples to examine biological variation. Such work can reveal population-level patterns, trauma, teeth, or disease, but results depend on preservation and sample size. They should not be converted into a diagnosis for everyone inside the atlas polygon.

Knives, awls, spoons, hide tools, hearths, and sleeping platforms supported ordinary bodily care as well as work. They could prepare food, clothing, warmth, and shelter. Archaeology cannot tell which implement treated an illness unless context or traces support that use, so the card avoids naming medical instruments.

The consulted exact-period evidence does not name healers, midwives, remedies, surgical procedures, or institutions. That silence reflects the limits of unwritten archaeology, not an absence of knowledge or compassion. People surely tended injuries and sickness, but who helped, what they used, and what they believed remain unsecured.

A central hearth reduced cold exposure and made hot food or water possible, while hide working produced protective clothing and bedding. Those are health-supporting technologies, not proof of a formal medical system. Warmth is excellent medicine for being cold; it is not a universal cure, despite every blanket’s ambitions.

Early medieval craniological and dental studies combine preserved individuals from several western Siberian burial series. Researchers can compare measured traits, but small or uneven samples cannot answer every question about illness or childhood. Fragile skeletal evidence deserves narrower claims, especially about the health of entire communities.

The polygon follows major Arctic rivers and estuaries, and many archaeological sites occupy river terraces. Waterways supplied fish, travel corridors, and nearby water. Site location does not reveal whether households drank directly, melted snow, stored water, or boiled it, so those daily steps remain open questions.

Published house descriptions identify hearths, entrances, platforms, posts, and storage features, but no standard indoor latrine securely dated across these communities. A mysterious pit should not be promoted to “toilet” without contents and context. Archaeological plumbing deserves evidence, even when children ask the best question first.

Fort ditches and ramparts managed defense and shaped runoff around some settlements. A ditch is not automatically a sewer: form, slope, fill, and connections matter. Calling every trench sanitation would be like calling every modern pothole a bathtub because both can contain water.

Cooking, craft, animals, broken pots, and fires produced bones, ash, fragments, dung, and other waste. Archaeologists study where deposits accumulated, yet the reviewed evidence does not establish one shared disposal rule. Practices probably differed between permanent forts, short camps, riverbanks, tundra, and forest.

Toilet verdict: people obviously relieved themselves, but no securely identified exact-period toilet can be generalized across this atlas label. Waste may have been carried away, deposited outside, or handled seasonally, but those options are not direct findings here. Missing pipes mean missing pipes, not missing hygiene.

No securely dated and localized Samoyedic-language writing from 700 to 800 is known in the consulted scholarship. Proto-Samoyedic forms are reconstructions made by comparing later languages, not words penned by an eighth-century speaker. This card therefore provides no fake alphabet, quotation, or decorative pseudo-inscription.

The earliest substantial documentation cited in linguistic histories consists of much later word lists, missionary work, and nineteenth-century grammars. Nenets, Selkup, and Nganasan writing systems were standardized only in the twentieth century. A later printed sample would be real language, but nonrepresentative of this exact century and polygon.

Fortifications, weapon displays, and unequal grave goods can suggest conflict, prestige, and organized labor. They do not reveal a king, tax system, capital, or law code governing Yamal through Taymyr. “State” is therefore a poor registry kind; “culture” better signals a cautious evidence umbrella.

At 1530 the atlas assigns only some former probes to Nenets, Enets, or Nganasan ids, while other probes have different owners or none. Those records begin more than seven centuries later and have separate lifetimes. Sharing this card with any one of them would invent a clean ethnic succession.

At 800 the exact id ends with no same-shape successor; all thirteen target probes revert to a broader forest umbrella. Families, languages, craft traditions, and local communities continued beyond the software seam. The atlas stops saying “Samoyèdes”; history does not press a giant Arctic off switch.

ending.text: The exact samoyedes id ends at 800 because the atlas removes its one broad polygon and restores the Finno-Ugric taiga hunter-gatherers label at every fixed target probe. Archaeological traditions continue beyond that date, and no evidence supports a simultaneous conquest, extinction, language shift, or political collapse. A separate broad Siberians repaint arrives in 1279. The much later Nenets, Enets, and Nganasan records divide only parts of the former geometry and begin in 1530; they are not safe one-to-one successors. This card therefore ends with continuing local communities, changing material traditions, movement, contact, and later identities rather than a fabricated handoff.
